title: Injustice, Lawlessness, and the Two Ways of God
english: This is a falsehood; for the Trinity possesses goodness essentially. Humans possess the good and the just and virtue through participation in the Trinity. Even if they themselves turn away, it exists. It exists in God, from which they have the capacity to be excellent. But evil, if it is not active, does not exist at all.

For this reason, many scriptures teach that it does not exist; from which it is concluded that there are neither two opposing principles in essence, nor are men bad by construction, as many heterodox people also desire, claiming that no one will choose either good or evil. Much that is absurd and impious follows from this. See: if all existing things are such by construction, and the wicked are so in essence, all legislation passes away; for the law cannot make the good good, nor the evil good. And if the law passes away, all exhortation, all encouragement, all counsel passes away, and the reason of man is entirely refuted; for he who does not have choice and will is not rational. And the coming of the Savior is superfluous. Does he make the good good? It is such from itself. But does he make the evil good? It is not of a nature to receive the participation of good. Therefore, the one sinning sins in vain.

For it is written in another psalm concerning that great one, the devil, the cause of all evil: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 74:6). We have said many times that the names lying against the opposing power are names of choice; for indeed, 'devil' is said, he is named 'Satan', which is 'the adversary', 'sinner'; and this name is a name of choice. And with the article, it is even more so itself: 'Behold, I have given you to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power' (Lk 10:19)—not of an enemy, but 'of the enemy'. And: 'Save us' (Mt 6:13)—not from an evil thing, but 'from the evil one'. And here: 'Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 74:6). Then it brings forth: 'His sin shall be sought, and it shall not be found through it.' Because of its own nature, it is not found. His sin is sometimes sought and is not found, not existing anywhere, not having moved to another place, but because of itself it is not found, since it does not have being by itself.

Unless in the one acting. And furthermore: 'and injustice lied about itself' (Ps 25:11). Here, to lie, we say in this way, as we often say the earth lies. Injustice therefore lies about itself, so as to no longer exist. It lied about itself because of its own nature. Thus, those who act lawlessly do so for no reason, not to gain something, but rather to be harmed. 'Make known to me your ways, O Lord' (Ps 25:4), those who act lawlessly without having experienced the law.

Now, concerning the written [word], regarding the law according to teaching, I say: for those not having received this are called lawless, as also in: 'blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven' (Ps 32:1). But sin after the law is not called simply lawlessness, but transgression: 'transgressions ensnare a man, and each one is constricted by the bands of his own sins' (Prov 5:22). 'Nor do the lawless persist before your eyes' (Ps 139:7). The lawless person never becomes an addition to God. Under the eyes of God, he does not become [so] except in a different way according to the word of providence. But according to the command of the diligent, they do not persist. They do not persist in the same way as the righteous, concerning whom it is said: 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Ps 34:15). Therefore, by saying 'they do not persist', he shows that they once were, when they were guarding the law, but when they have become transgressors of it, then they have been cast out from the eyes of God.

'Make known to me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Lead me into your truth' (Ps 25:4-5). The ways of God are said to be twofold: either those leading toward Him, or those which He Himself walks, proceeding through all things, as is necessary according to the word of providence or according to benefiting and being in His receptive ones. For he says: 'I will dwell in them and walk about' (Ps 15:2). But he who walks about has paths, which He Himself walks. Thus, we call the ways of God either those leading toward Him—and these are the virtues—or those which He Himself treads according to His providence and judgment and administration and gift. It is therefore necessary to know the ways of God by Him making them known. 'And teach me your paths' (Ps 25:4). That is, those which those hurrying toward You [tread], or those which You tread, proceeding through the works of Your grace. If there are even more to say: you know that before teaching, something must be known; for from pre-known things come understandings and scientific proofs. Both...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Eternal Age and Repentance
english: Therefore make known to me your ways; for in this manner I shall learn your paths, following those who have worn them down, those who have proceeded in the good things or those who have proceeded because you proceeded, having a subscript and a pattern, 'that we may follow your footsteps' (Ps 25:4). Therefore, to know precedes to teach. Thus it is said that demonstrations and teachings come from things already known. It can be understood in this way: that common concepts are pre-known. And indeed, when we test a teaching, we say we are testing it in reference to common concepts.

For indeed, at times a teacher says something, and the common concept of the learner pre-perceives and knows whether he speaks well or not. You will find even in these human, scientific demonstrations, that sciences are not being led well if those listening do not pre-perceive what it is necessary to pre-perceive. For indeed, this has often been said to us: that when someone learns something that must be foreknown before the instruction, it is not right to speak to him through obscure words, since it is not familiar to him. 'Guide me into the truth' (Ps 27:11).

After the practical virtues and the guidance according to disposition, the guidance into the truth occurs; for, he says, 'desiring wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you' (Ps 119:2). And wisdom and truth are the same. The Savior, indeed, is said to be both: 'Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24). And he himself said: 'I am the truth' (John 14:6).

And teach me, that you are my God and Savior. You are my God, having created me; you are my Savior, willing that I should improve. Therefore, become my teacher. As Creator, so also [become] teacher. And I waited for you all the day. I waited for you all the time of my life, so that I might have you as teacher and Savior; for 'toward you' I 'lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1), not toward another. I did not entreat another, so that you might make known to me your ways and teach me your paths, but I deemed you worthy to become teacher of these things to me.

Often the whole of our life's time is called 'a day', according to what has been said: 'for your sake we are dying all the day' (Ps 116:3), instead of what the apostle has made 'every day' (2 Cor 6:13). And 'a day' can be said to be the whole time of the life of the saints, because they are always in light, being illuminated by the tru[th].

The thin light of 'the sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:8). This day is not interrupted by nights; it is continuous. For it is said in the Psalm: 'our age is for the illumination of your face' (Ps 36:9). And the life which is extended by the sojourn here is called an age; for it is said, 'there shall be to you a servant for an age' (Ps 119:9), and 'I shall not eat meat for an age' (Ps 119:119), instead of 'through life'. Since therefore the time of our life's day has come to illuminate your face—for we have come to pre-announce your presence—our whole age has become for the illumination of your face because of the illuminating and making manifest to men your visitation.

Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassions, because they are from eternity. For even if I have entreated and lifted my soul to you and desired other things to be present to me from you, I do not ask these things according to merit. You provide these things mercifully and compassionately in accordance with the one: 'not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16); for even if we have done all things from ourselves, by the mercy of God we strive to attain their end. Hear me as a merciful one, and as a compassionate one receive my prayers. 'And your compassions, because they are from eternity'. For it is not yesterday and the morning that I began to be compassionate. You are eternal, you are eternally good.

Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances (Ps 25:7). You see that concerning former ignorances and sins one prays for mercy and the compassion of God; for there is no longer repentance sending back a prayer upon committed sins. Repentances happen upon things passed away. For it says: 'do not remember the sins and the ignorances of me' (Ps 25:7) which I have, and now I do not have, but those of youth. And it is possible even thus: whatever the age of the one ignoring and sinning may be, he is young in the youth of his mind, in the newness of his conduct. It is possible, therefore, to always find those who confess and bring words of repentance concerning sins passed away, doing this: 'we have sinned, we have transgressed, we have been ungodly' (1 John 1:8); for how is it possible? The one repenting asks for virtue. How then can one who is still in sins have or receive virtue? 'Turn away' (Ps 34:14) therefore 'from evil and do good'. According to your mercy, remember me. What about 'remember me'? It is a personal idiom of the Scripture instead of 'know me' (Ps 139:1).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Testimony and Divine Glory
english: Because of your goodness, Lord, not because of my own virtue do you remember me. The Lord is good and upright; he who is with uprightness is good. For often 'good' is taken in a sense of deception: 'bad associations corrupt good morals' (Prov 13:20). Thus, 'good' is not taken here in a praiseworthy sense, but in a sense of being easy or indulgent. Similarly with 'innocent': 'the innocent believes every word,' instead of meaning 'the well-disposed.' And regarding heretics, Paul writes: 'by flattering speech and blessing they deceive the hearts of the innocent' (2 Cor 11:14). Because of this, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way.

If he were abrupt, if he were not good, he would not establish laws in the way of salvation for those sinning, but would hand them over to be punished. Therefore, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way, so that having traveled this way, they may possess salvation. And observe: he does not say 'those who have sinned,' but 'those sinning.' And those still sinning, through exhortations, admonitions, and laws, he leads into the way. But how can the written word mean this, considering all the implications of the law?

He will guide the gentle in judgment. Having judged, he guides the gentle; for again, gentleness often signifies indulgence. But when they are guided having been judged, they possess a perfect virtue, which the Savior taught them to have, saying: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart' (Matt 11:29). And 'in judgment' can also be understood thus: judging these gentle ones to be capable of being benefited, he guides them. And the first interpretation is most in harmony with the text: that having been judged, they come upon the way having God as a guide. Or does he not guide, he who says: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle' (Matt 11:29)?

All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. In many places of the Scriptures, mercy is joined with truth. How great is the truth, so that I might say, it is above men. And observe that all things rational, and all things transcendent, and all things above, require truth. Here, however, we require mercy, so that we may be able to know the truth. It has been said in the previous sections: 'Guide me in your truth, O Lord, and in your paths' (Ps 25:5). Therefore, the beginning of walking these blessed ways is from mercy.

It becomes a part of God, and an end from the truth. [This is] for those who search out His covenant and His testimonies, not for those who search simply, but specifically those who search out [them]. Those searching the Scriptures, they too are searching out the covenant of God. To search and to seek out are the same thing.

"And His testimonies": His testimonies are the words testified by Him. You know that what has been testified is irrefutable. Therefore, the irrefutable is often signified by the name of 'testimonies' regarding the divine instructions. What? That which He Himself testified? That which He Himself confirmed. And it is possible to call things irrefutable and unshakeable testimonies, not because they were testified by someone, but because their nature is such that they testify by the truth.

"And the witness," He says, "is faithful in heaven." Concerning God, if it is said that God testifies, we do not mean that the one testifying establishes Him. John came "that he might testify about the light" (John 1:7); for John, the one testifying about the light, did not provide faith and standing to the light. The one testifying shows himself to be knowing by his knowledge, and the one testifying is shown to be diligent by his virtue. So also those who have been well-pleasing and have struggled in persecutions are called witnesses as is fitting. They showed themselves to be lovers of truth, they showed themselves to be knowers of the truth. They did not confirm the truth, but they confirmed themselves. Therefore, those things worthy of the one testifying are often called testimonies.

"For your name's sake, O Lord. Not for the sake of our diligence or our life, but because of your name. This indeed is said in another psalm: 'Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory' (Psalm 115:1); for we are enriched by you and you were named our God, so do it for your name's sake. "And atone for my sin; for it is great." We say "it is great" in this way: if so many paths have been made known to Him, and He has been led to the truth, how much sin does He have? It has been said before [the next part]: "Cleanse me from my secret sins" (Psalm 51:2), because even a small stain is a great sin to the one who is entirely cleansed.
"Who is the man who fears the Lord?" Therefore, he asks: who then is the man who fears God? To this one "he will teach in the way in which..."
